options: Supplies and a new governor, crops that fed it, and tobacco
A shipment of gold and silver found upriver from the fort
A treaty with Powhatan that ended every quarrel for good
The arrival of Sir Walter Raleigh with a hundred more settlers

items.stem: True or false: Sir Walter Raleigh sailed to Roanoke Island himself and led the colony there.
options: True
False
justify_options: The chapter says he never journeyed to the New World; he organized and paid for the two attempts
The chapter says he led the first attempt of 1585 himself and then handed the second one over to John White
The chapter says he stayed away three years because the fighting with Spain kept his ships in England

items.stem: What does the chapter say about the roughly twenty Africans a Dutch ship landed in Virginia in 1619?
options: They were sold as slaves the day the ship reached Virginia
They were carried on to the Caribbean a few weeks later
They were free sailors who chose to stay in the colony
They appear to have been treated as indentured servants

items.stem: What was an indentured servant, as the chapter explains the term?
options: Someone who was paid wages by the Virginia Company
Someone who worked a few years to pay for the crossing
Someone who worked for a master for the whole of his life
Someone who owned land and rented it out to other farmers

items.stem: Which empire did Mansa Musa rule, and where did he travel in the early 1300s?
options: Songhai, and he sailed south with the Portuguese
Ghana, and he crossed the Sahara to trade for salt
Mali, and he made a pilgrimage to Mecca
Timbuktu, and he traveled to the coast to meet traders

items.stem: What does the chapter say created a market for slaves from West Africa?
options: The tribal wars fought along the western coast of Africa
European and American demand for cheap labor
The Portuguese need for sailors aboard their ships
A shortage of gold in the empire of Songhai

items.stem: Who is considered the first African in America?
options: Esteban, a Moroccan slave of a Spanish explorer
Mansa Musa, the ruler of the empire of Mali
Zheng He, an admiral of the Ming dynasty
One of the twenty Africans landed in Virginia in 1619

items.stem: What happened to Esteban's party after their makeshift boats capsized near Galveston?
options: Natives held them captive until only four were left
A Spanish ship picked them up again within a few weeks
They founded a small settlement and stayed on that coast
They walked back to Cuba along the coast within a year

items.stem: How does the chapter contrast a slave with an indentured servant?
options: A slave cost about the same but could buy his freedom back
A slave was paid wages while a servant worked for nothing
A slave worked in the fields while a servant worked indoors
A slave cost about five times as much and served for life

items.stem: How did Mansa Musa's wealth affect other civilizations?
options: His spending on the way to Mecca upset economies, Egypt's worst
His armies took Timbuktu and Gao away from the rulers of Songhai
His gold paid for the Portuguese caravels that first sailed to India
His pilgrimage opened a new trade route between Mali and the Indies

items.stem: The chapter says the transatlantic slave trade exploded when Europeans arrived. How does it explain that?
options: Barbary pirates seized whole villages and sold them in the Americas
Buyers wanted cheap labor, so Africans raided to meet the demand
The Portuguese made slaveholding a condition of every trade deal
African rulers ran out of gold and sold captives to replace it

items.stem: The chapter says it is uncertain how the first people reached the Americas. What is one possible route it gives?
options: A crossing from the coast of western Africa
A land bridge that linked Asia to Alaska
A voyage with the Viking ships about AD 1000
A chain of islands running down from Iceland

items.stem: Where does the chapter's account of people spreading over the earth begin?
options: With the call of Abraham to go to a new land
With the flood of Noah and the ark on Ararat
With the exodus of Israel out of the land of Egypt
With the confusing of languages at Babel

items.stem: How does the chapter say the native peoples showed the capabilities God gives every image-bearer?
options: They gathered into one nation under a single powerful chief
They set aside forests where nobody was allowed to hunt at all
They kept careful written records of everything their tribes had done
They shaped their environments skillfully and built lasting works
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Native American Culture and Religion

items.stem: What was the Middle Passage?
options: The sale of captives to slave owners in the Americas
The march that carried captives to the coast of Africa
The ocean crossing that carried captives to the Americas
The overland route that carried salt south across the Sahara

items.stem: Why does the chapter say 'perhaps' about the land bridge instead of stating it as settled fact?
options: It says how and when the first people arrived is uncertain
It says the Bible names the exact route the first people traveled
It says only the Vikings ever crossed from one side to the other
It says the land bridge melted before anyone could cross over it

items.stem: Europeans often called the native peoples backward or savage. What does the chapter say they were failing to see?
options: The number of warriors each tribe could put into the field
The treaties the tribes had already signed with the Spanish
The wealth in gold and silver that the tribes had gathered up
The abilities God gives to everyone who bears His image
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Native American Culture and Religion

items.stem: True or false: the chapter says slave traders packed as many people as they could onto a ship in order to make as much money as possible.
options: True
False
justify_options: People lay stacked on one another or chained side by side with no room to move
Ships carried few captives at a time so that the healthy ones would fetch a higher price
Traders fed the captives rice, cornmeal, or yams twice a day to keep them strong enough

question_sets.label: Explorers and what each one did

shared_options.theme: a hunt for the golden cities of Cíbola that ended in the Southwest
shared_options.correction: the Spaniard who rode north from Mexico in 1540 after Cíbola's golden cities, found the adobe villages of the Pueblo instead, and was the first European to see the Grand Canyon

shared_options.theme: a march through the Southeast that ended at a great river
shared_options.correction: the conquistador who started from Florida in 1539 hoping for riches in Indian settlements and traveled the Southeast until he came upon the Mississippi River

shared_options.theme: the first Spanish exploration of Florida
shared_options.correction: the first Spaniard to explore Florida, arriving in 1513 in search of riches, and possibly the first European to see land that is now the United States

shared_options.theme: French exploration of the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes
shared_options.correction: the French explorer called the Father of New France, who explored the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes region and built the fort that became the city of Quebec

shared_options.theme: English raids on Spanish ports and a voyage on around the world
shared_options.correction: the most famous Sea Dog, who plundered Spanish ports, escaped by sailing on around South America and across the Pacific, and was knighted aboard the Golden Hind

shared_options.theme: paying for English colonies without ever sailing to them
shared_options.correction: the English nobleman who organized and financed the two Roanoke expeditions of 1585 and 1587 but never journeyed to the New World himself

questions.focus: a search for the legendary golden cities of Cíbola
questions.stem: In 1540 this explorer came north from Mexico hunting the legendary golden cities of Cíbola. He never found them, but he did find the adobe villages of the Pueblo Indians, and he was the first European to see the Grand Canyon. Who was he?

questions.focus: an inland march through the Southeast that ended at a great river
questions.stem: Hoping to find riches in the Indian settlements of North America, this Spaniard started out from Florida in 1539 and traveled through the Southeast until he came upon the Mississippi River. Who was he?

questions.focus: the first Spanish exploration of Florida
questions.stem: This Spaniard arrived in 1513, searching for riches among other things, and was the first of his countrymen to explore Florida. The chapter adds that he may have been the first European to see land that is now the United States. Who was he?

questions.focus: French exploration of the St. Lawrence, and a fort that grew into a city
questions.stem: This explorer has been called the Father of New France. He further explored the St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes region, and he built the fort that later became the city of Quebec. Who was he?

questions.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Armada
questions.focus: raiding Spanish ports and then sailing on around the world to escape
questions.stem: In 1577 this English captain sailed down the coast of South America, plundering Spanish ports and capturing treasure ships. To escape the Spanish patrols he kept going — around South America, across the Pacific, and around Africa's Cape of Good Hope — and came home to a triumphant welcome. Who was he?

questions.focus: paying for two colonies without ever crossing the ocean
questions.stem: This English nobleman, another favorite of the queen, organized two colonizing expeditions to Roanoke Island — one in 1585 and another in 1587 — although he never journeyed to the New World himself. Who was he?

shared_options.theme: pushing inland after treasure and planting a church wherever land was claimed
shared_options.correction: the Europeans whose conquistadors pushed inland after treasure, who began colonizing Mexico as early as 1519, and who established their language, customs, and Roman Catholic religion in the lands they claimed

shared_options.theme: fur trading from forts and posts along the rivers and lakes
shared_options.correction: the Europeans who settled the St. Lawrence and Mississippi and the Great Lakes, traded tools and clothing for furs, and built forts, missions, and trading posts instead of organized towns

shared_options.theme: an early claim to the Atlantic coast, and captains who preyed on Spanish shipping
shared_options.correction: the Europeans whose claim to the Atlantic coast dates from John Cabot in 1497 and whose Sea Dogs raided Spanish harbors and treasure ships through the 1500s

shared_options.theme: the ship design and the voyages that made long-distance exploration possible
shared_options.correction: the Europeans who adapted small fishing boats into the fast ships called caravels, sailed down and around Africa toward India, and later joined the trade of the Songhai empire

shared_options.theme: northern seamen who reached America centuries before Columbus
shared_options.correction: the Norsemen of northern Europe, who planted colonies in Iceland and Greenland and reached Newfoundland about AD 1000, though the rest of Europe never heard of the voyages

questions.focus: conquistadors hunting treasure inland, and a language and a church planted in the claimed lands
questions.stem: Their conquistadors pushed inland from the coasts hunting treasure, they began to colonize Mexico as early as 1519, and wherever they claimed land they established their language, their customs, and their Roman Catholic religion. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: using the rivers and lakes as roads into the interior for the fur trade
questions.stem: They settled along the St. Lawrence and Mississippi Rivers and around the Great Lakes, using the water as roads into the interior. They traded axes, pots, and clothing to the Indians for the skins of beavers, foxes, otters, and moose, and they built forts and trading posts rather than towns. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

questions.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Armada
questions.focus: an early claim to the Atlantic coast, followed by captains who raided Spanish shipping
questions.stem: As early as 1497 one of their explorers laid claim to the Atlantic coast of North America, and through the 1500s their sea captains raided Spanish harbors and seized treasure ships. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: the ship design that let Europeans sail far from shore
questions.stem: Before the 1400s few Europeans went far out to sea, because their ships could not handle rough conditions away from the shore. These people solved that by adapting small fishing boats for long-distance travel with specially designed sails, producing the fast ships called caravels. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: reaching North America about AD 1000, unknown to the rest of Europe
questions.stem: Seamen out of northern Europe, they planted colonies in Iceland and Greenland and then sailed west to Canada about AD 1000. The rest of Europe never learned of those voyages. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

question_sets.label: Indian regions and the tribes that lived in them
question_sets.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → The People of North America

shared_options.theme: desert farming and homes made of cliff rock, dried clay, and logs
shared_options.correction: the region of the Pueblo, Apache, Hopi, and Navajo, whose people farmed the desert, gathered wild plants, hunted small animals, and built cliff houses, adobe homes, and hogans

shared_options.theme: mounds of earth raised for tombs and religious ceremonies
shared_options.correction: the region of the mound builders and of the Cherokee, Seminole, and Creek, where earthen mounds served as tombs and ceremonial sites and Cahokia held more people in 1200 than London did

shared_options.theme: making everything a family needs out of what the frozen north supplies
shared_options.correction: the region near the Arctic Circle where the Inuit shaped igloos from snow and ice and hunted caribou, whales, seals, and walruses for food, clothing, light, and boat skins

shared_options.theme: forest tribes whose steady crops let them build permanent villages
shared_options.correction: the region from the Atlantic to the Mississippi where the Algonquian, Huron, Iroquois, and Powhatan hunted, fished, and planted maize, squash, and tobacco, living in wigwams and longhouses

questions.focus: the tribes of the dry country and the three ways they fed themselves
questions.stem: The Pueblo, the Apache, the Hopi, and the Navajo lived here. They farmed the desert, gathered wild plants, and hunted small animals, and the region is known for turquoise jewelry, pottery, and woven goods. Which region does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: the tribes of the region where earthen mounds were raised
questions.stem: The Cherokee, the Seminole, and the Creek lived here, in the same part of the country as the people who raised mounds of earth for tombs and religious ceremonies. Which region does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: hunting the animals of the frozen north for everything a family needed
questions.stem: The people here hunted caribou, whales, seals, and walruses for food and clothing. They burned whale oil for light and stretched the skins of hunted animals over their small boats and kayaks. Which region does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: the region the Powhatan of Virginia belonged to
questions.stem: The Powhatan lived in villages along the rivers of Virginia, where they fished, hunted, and farmed, and where the English later built Jamestown. The chapter groups them with the tribes of one of its seven regions. Which region is it?
